extracted.intended_audience: general readers, viewers, media researchers, and producers interested in Last Week Tonight or satirical news programming
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for producing and evaluating a weekly news-satire/late-night show segment that combines comedy with in-depth, fact-based examination of political or social issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main-segment long-form focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Each episode's main segment covers one political or social issue in length, even if it may not have received recent news coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize a single in-depth topic per episode that allows exploration of context and complexity rather than brief topical jokes; the main segment may occupy most or all of the episode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementary short segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Each episode contains a small handful of shorter segments and then one main segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use shorter, recent-news-oriented pieces to complement the episode's longer investigation; occasionally omit short segments so the main piece fills the entire runtime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend of humor styles with fact-based content
rubrics_metrics.description: Alongside satire, the show uses self-referential humor, black comedy and observational comedy, and has been noted for its informative and fact-based content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine varied comedic approaches while grounding arguments in factual reporting and research to lend credibility and informative value to the comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep-dive/purpose: systemic contextualization
rubrics_metrics.description: The show takes deeper dives into systemic issues which intend to illustrate both the wider socio-political context and the complex interconnections and embeddedness of public policies in social outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame topics to reveal structural causes and interconnections rather than only individual anecdotes or surface-level satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive media monitoring in preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparations involve watching everything and monitoring many outlets with the aim of 'how to see a story told badly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive review of multiple news sources (TV, cable, online) is used to identify poorly told stories and potential targets for deeper, corrective satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of old or overcovered news
rubrics_metrics.description: Concern about dealing with old news: 'If something happens on a Monday... there's probably barely a point in doing it ... attracted to stories that are off the grid ... may end up skewing more international.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer topics that still have fresh angles or underreported international/off-grid stories rather than rehashing thoroughly covered breaking news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of produced comedy elements as internal breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct little, produced comedy elements that serve the function of commercial breaks throughout the show, allowing the program to get out of the studio, get away from the host's voice and break the show up a bit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design short produced pieces to change pacing and tone, maintain audience attention, and create variety during a long monologue-style presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: No parody correspondents
rubrics_metrics.description: The show is 'not going to be a parody news show, so no people pretending to be journalists.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid recurring correspondents who act as faux journalists; keep the format focused on the host and produced segments rather than parody reporter bits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to criticize corporate/host network entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Oliver has stated that he has 'full creative freedom, including free rein to criticize corporations', and frequently pokes fun at HBO's (now former) parent company AT&T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain editorial independence to allow open criticism of powerful entities, including network partners, when relevant to the subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title-sequence satirical design
rubrics_metrics.description: The show's title sequence presents images relating to the world at large with satirical captions written in dog Latin (e.g., photo labels like 'hostus mostus').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a stylized, satirical title sequence to set tone and convey the show's satirical worldview before the episode begins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of visual aids and on-screen graphics
rubrics_metrics.description: The show includes a panel in the upper-left corner that frequently displays a photo or graphic as a comedic aid; a full-screen graphic will show and play a video clip when Oliver is citing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy on-screen images, panels, and full-screen clips to illustrate points, provide comedic juxtaposition, and present evidence or citations visually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video compilations and segues
rubrics_metrics.description: Oliver's speech is broken up with video compilations of recent news clips, or recurring segments, into which Oliver segues by saying, 'And now, this.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interleave curated clip montages and recurring beats to support arguments and create rhythmic transitions; use a recognizable segue phrase to signal these shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mock trailers and parody commercials
rubrics_metrics.description: Oliver has ended some segments with mock trailers for fictional TV shows or commercials that satirize the subject of his speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create parody trailers or faux-advertising segments to lampoon targets and provide variety in satirical modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring mascots and physical comedy props
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurring element of the show is Oliver's use of mascots (e.g., Jeff the Diseased Lung, Hoots the NSA Owl, Taryn the Tinder Chicken) and Last Week Tonight puppets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop memorable mascots/props to personify issues, create shareable visuals, and sustain running jokes across episodes and campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hashtag and social-media virality strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: He often coins hashtags related to his segment for use in social media, some of which go viral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentionally create catchy social hooks (hashtags, slogans) tied to segments to encourage sharing and amplify real-world engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest selection and roles
rubrics_metrics.description: The show frequently features one or more celebrity guests in segments to help Oliver get his point across; guests have given monologues, been interviewed, played musical numbers, participated in skits, or starred in parody PSAs; guests may appear live or via pre-recorded clips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select guests for substantive contribution to a segment's argument or comedic effect rather than mere star power; use multiple guest formats to vary presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviewing affected or expert individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Oliver has interviewed personalities who were directly involved in or impacted by the issues being discussed to get their first-hand experiences and viewpoints (e.g., Edward Snowden, Dalai Lama, Anita Hill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include primary-source interviews with experts, victims, or participants to add credibility, humanize issues, and deepen the audience's understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of publicity stunts to illustrate structural problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Segments have used stunts to demonstrate regulatory or systemic issues (e.g., creating 'Our Lady of Perpetual Exemption' to show how 'disturbingly easy' it is to set up a tax-exempt religious organization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design demonstrative stunts that reveal loopholes or absurdities in institutions, while ensuring legal/ethical considerations are addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of campaign-style marketing to amplify segments
rubrics_metrics.description: The program has amplified segments via marketing tactics: promoting mascots, sending shirts/billboards, encouraging hashtags, and creating downloadable content for fan use (e.g., green-screen zebra footage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pair on-air content with off-air promotional materials and interactive assets to encourage audience participation and spread the message beyond broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic online distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The show posts main segments and extended clips to a YouTube channel and sometimes creates 'Web Exclusives'; timing of uploads (next-day vs delayed) is part of release strategy and can be adjusted by season or platform rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage online video platforms to reach broader audiences, tailor release timing to platform and rights constraints, and produce web-only content to maintain engagement between broadcasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential to catalyze real-world action ('John Oliver effect')
rubrics_metrics.description: On several occasions, show segments have been followed by real-world change and action by the public, policymakers and/or institutions (e.g., net neutrality comments to the FCC, crowdfunding for public-defender offices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design segments with calls to action or awareness-raising elements when appropriate, recognizing that high-profile satire can mobilize public response and policy attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial voice: 'comedy first' but journalistic trappings
rubrics_metrics.description: Although some outlets have described Oliver's reporting as journalism or investigative journalism, Oliver states 'it's not journalism, it's comedy—it's comedy first, and it's comedy second.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep comedic intent primary while using rigorous research and evidence; avoid presenting the program as a substitute for formal journalism even when investigative techniques are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility in production logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: The show adapted production during the COVID-19 pandemic (filmed at home, virtual production) and later resumed studio filming; HBO allowed freedom in guests and elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to adapt production methods (remote filming, altered pacing) in response to external constraints while maintaining core format and standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and legal consideration awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Segments have prompted legal pushback (defamation lawsuits, censorship) and raised questions about ethical representation (e.g., claims of mischaracterization by corporations), indicating legal and reputational risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct careful fact-checking and legal review for potentially defamatory or risky claims; plan for responses to pushback and possible censorship in different international markets.
